risk.rationale: I rated it high: - E-WORK-START is the write that creates a work item and starts agents (JR-01). It is CSRF-bound and carries an idempotency key and a case revision (INV-REVISION, handoff.md:3915-3947). A duplicate start, or a start on the wrong case, is hard to undo. - The case now comes from a chosen option or a fixed line (D-START-INTAKE r1), so wrong case resolution is a real failure mode. - The feature also edits the shared shell (`src/shell/TopNav.tsx`, `PhoneBar.tsx`) and repoints the shared contract types for every lane. Surfaces: - `ui`: SCR-04 and CMP-23 on both bars. - `api`: E-LINES, E-LINE-OPTIONS and E-WORK-START. - `security`: CSRF, never offering a line or option the API did not return, and nothing derived from roles. - `contract-change`: the consumer side of the D-START-INTAKE proposal and the v4 to v6 repoint. Excluded surfaces: - `payments`: money fields and payroll are out. - `auth`: the feature uses the existing session. - `dependency`: no packages are added. Product acceptance is required: - this is a new flow for the client; - minutes and change are built without their approved proof field; - the "can't start here yet" copy (PMO-0-6) has no board.

findings.summary: After a definitive 403 or 404 the form unlocks but keeps the same idempotency key. If the person then changes the project or a field and presses start, the same key goes out with a different body. That is the opposite of what the spec's assumption promises ("the same key is only ever resent with the same body"). On a backend that records keys before its permission or case check, it would also give a confusing 409 `idempotency_key_reused`. The spec only requires a new key after a 409 or 422, so this is a gap, not a contract break. Expected: a new key after any definitive 4xx, because nothing was written. Actual: `useStartWork.ts:186-208` makes a new key only in the 422 and 409 branches.

Whether a retry is safe depends on the order of the backend's checks, and the contract doesn't fix that order. Suppose the first POST did start and its answer was lost. "Check again" then only works if the backend looks up the idempotency key before it checks `case_revision` and the line grant. If it checks the revision first, a start that already happened, and moved the revision on, answers 409 `stale_revision`. The drawer would then unlock with a new key, and the next press would start the same work twice. The mock checks the key first (`mock/start-work.mjs:184-199`, though the line grant comes before the key). Also, any replay answer other than 201, for example a 200, shows as "uncertain" for good (`useStartWork.ts:181`). Please add both points to the PMO-0-1 question in build.md: look up the key first, then answer with the stored 201.

Some tests still name old contract versions. `tests/mock-work-list.test.ts:15` still reads `architecture/packages/v3/openapi.json` for E-WORK-LIST. The test name at `tests/mock-decide.test.ts:206` still says "v4" but validates through `OPENAPI_PATH`, which is now v6. Neither file is in F-05's lane, and the spec's 5-file repoint list doesn't cover them. Still, after the repoint there should be one contract version. Fix this in whichever lane owns those tests, or when rebasing onto F-06, F-07 or F-08.

A 201 is trusted without checking its body. `useStartWork.ts:180` casts `data` and reads `work_id`. With an empty 201 body (`data` undefined), it throws a TypeError out of `submit`: the error isn't caught and the drawer shows nothing. With no `work_id`, the browser goes to `/work/undefined`. Expected: a 201 without a string `work_id` is treated as uncertain.

The rebase isn't done yet. Base 2443664 isn't on `main`, and F-06, F-07 and F-08 haven't merged yet (their feature.json state is not merged). So the spec's rule that "every fixture, theirs included, must pass mock-contract against v6" can only be checked after the rebase. Re-run `tests/mock-contract.test.ts` and `tests/api-schema-drift.test.ts` after the rebase, before merging.

The same-origin check on `journey_url` can be bypassed. `safePath` (`frontend/src/features/start-work/LineForm.tsx:120-122`) checks the raw string with `startsWith('/')` and rejects `//` and `/\`. Browsers' URL parsers strip ASCII tab and newline before resolving, so `"/\t/evil.example"` and `"/\n/evil.example"` pass the check but resolve to `http://evil.example/`. I confirmed this with `new URL("/\t/evil.example", "http://localhost:3511").href`. Next's `Link` treats a non-local URL as external, so the click goes off-site. The value comes from our own E-LINES (v6 types it only as `string, minLength 1`), so the risk is a bad or compromised server value. But round 2 claims and tests this rule, and the coordinator named it as high-risk. Expected: resolve before comparing, e.g. `const u = new URL(url, window.location.origin); return u.origin === window.location.origin ? u.pathname + u.search + u.hash : undefined`, or reject any control character. Also add `'/\t/elsewhere.example'` and `'/\n/elsewhere.example'` to the `it.each` at `tests/start-work.test.tsx:646`.

findings.summary: `safePath` (frontend/src/features/start-work/LineForm.tsx:120-122) lets through a path whose second character is a tab, CR or LF. Example: `"/\t/evil.example"` or `"/\n\\evil.example"`. Browsers strip those characters while parsing the URL, so the link resolves off-site. `node -e 'new URL("/\t/evil.example","http://localhost:3511/").href'` prints `http://evil.example/`. Expected: link only when `new URL(url, window.location.origin).origin === window.location.origin`, or accept only `^/(?![/\\])` with no ASCII control characters or whitespace anywhere. Add that case to the "not a same-origin path" test at tests/start-work.test.tsx:646. This can only be reached through a bad or compromised E-LINES value, so it is low risk.

`safePath` (`frontend/src/features/start-work/LineForm.tsx:121-130`) still lets some values link to another site. The origin check runs on the resolved URL. But the function then returns `resolved.pathname + resolved.search + resolved.hash`, and the URL parser can normalise a same-origin URL's path into one that starts with `//`. Next's `Link` (`LineForm.tsx:146`) then renders that as a protocol-relative href to another host. I ran the exact function body in node with origin `http://localhost:3501`. `"/.//evil.example"`, `"/a/..//evil.example"` and `"http://localhost:3501//evil.example"` all return `"//evil.example"`, and `new URL("//evil.example", origin).href` is `http://evil.example/`. Expected: return `resolved.href`, which is absolute and same-origin, so it can't be read as protocol-relative. Or return `undefined` when `resolved.pathname.startsWith('//')`. Add `'/.//evil.example'` to the `safePath` refused list (`tests/start-work.test.tsx:680`), or assert that it maps to a same-origin href. This is the same risk as TECH-2-1 (a bad or compromised E-LINES value), so it keeps the same severity.

The same-origin check can still be beaten, now through dot segments. `safePath` (`frontend/src/features/start-work/LineForm.tsx:121-130`) checks `resolved.origin === origin` and then returns `resolved.pathname + resolved.search + resolved.hash`. The parser collapses `.` and `..` segments, so `new URL("/.//evil.example", origin).pathname` is `"//evil.example"`. The origin matches, so that string goes to `<Link href>` at `LineForm.tsx:146`, and the browser reads it as protocol-relative: `http://evil.example/`. I ran an exact copy of the function in node: `safePath("/.//evil.example","http://localhost:3511")` returned `//evil.example`. `/..//evil.example`, `/a/..//evil.example`, `/%2e//evil.example` and `/%2e%2e//evil.example` do the same. Round 2's raw-string check passed `/.//evil.example` through unchanged, and a browser resolves that as a same-origin path, so this bypass is new in this round. Expected: return `resolved.href`, which is an absolute same-origin URL (Next's `Link` treats a same-origin absolute URL as local). Or refuse when `resolved.pathname.startsWith('//')`. Then add `'/.//evil.example'`, `'/..//evil.example'` and `'/%2e//evil.example'` to the refused `it.each` at `frontend/tests/start-work.test.tsx:680` and to the component `it.each` at `:700`. The risk is the same as TECH-2-1: only a bad or compromised E-LINES value can reach it, and the mock sends only `"/projects"`. It is blocking because this round claims and tests this exact rule and leaves a working bypass.
